title: A team is available
text: A start-up in {city} has run out of money. Its engineering team is excellent and about to scatter.

opts.label: Hire the whole team
opts.hint: Pay off their investors and take all four.

out.text: They join as a unit, with their own way of doing things.

opts.label: Pass
opts.hint: You have a hiring plan already.

lesson: Buying a team is faster than building one, and brings a ready-made culture — which may or may not be yours.

title: A government tender
text: A public body in {city} is tendering a multi-year contract. The paperwork alone is a project.

opts.label: Bid low
opts.hint: Win on price; live with the margin.

out.text: You win. The work is steady and thin.
They choose quality. A fine contract.

opts.label: No bid
opts.hint: Public contracts are more trouble than they are worth.

lesson: In a sealed-bid auction the winner is often whoever most underestimated the cost. Decide what the work is worth before deciding what wins.

title: An innovation grant
text: A public fund is offering non-dilutive grants for research in your field.
lesson: Grant money costs no equity and no interest. Its price is paperwork and time — cheap for an early-stage company.

title: An unsolicited term sheet
text: A fund you have never spoken to has sent an offer. They have clearly done their homework.

opts.label: Take it
opts.hint: Sell 15% at a 30% premium to your valuation.

out.text: The money arrives. So does a new board member.
They agree to 8% at a 50% premium.

lesson: Money offered when you do not need it comes on better terms than money sought when you do. Dilution is still dilution.

title: An invitation to speak
text: The industry’s main event wants you on the main stage.

out.text: They are delighted, and good at it.

opts.label: Decline
opts.hint: You have a company to run.

lesson: The founder’s time is the scarcest resource in the company. Visibility is worth some of it.

title: A big brand wants your product under its name
text: A household name wants to sell what you make in {city}, with their logo on it.

opts.label: Accept
opts.hint: Big volume, no brand credit, one powerful customer.

lesson: White-label volume fills capacity but builds someone else’s brand, and hands them your biggest account.

title: Renewal time
text: Your white-label partner is renewing. They would like 20% off, and have a second supplier lined up.
lesson: A customer who owns the brand owns the relationship. You were always replaceable; now you know the price.

title: Your lender wants out
text: The bank holding {loan} is shrinking its book and will take 95 cents on the dollar for early repayment of 30%.

opts.label: Take the discount
opts.hint: Use cash to retire debt cheaply.

lesson: Retiring debt at a discount is a guaranteed return. Compare it with what the same cash would earn inside the business.

title: A founder wants to sell
text: The owner of a small competitor is retiring and would rather sell to you than to a fund.

opts.label: Take a look
opts.hint: Put it on the deals list.

out.text: The numbers are on your desk.

lesson: Acquisitions look easy on the day you sign. The value is made or lost in the diligence before and the integration after.

title: A trade delegation
text: Officials from a city you have never looked at are in town and would like to pitch you on opening there.

opts.label: Host them
opts.hint: Lunch and a morning of your time.

out.text: They leave you a thick folder of market data.

lesson: Information about new markets has a price. Occasionally someone else pays it for you.

title: Security certification
text: Enterprise buyers keep asking for an independent security certification. The audit takes two quarters.

opts.label: Get certified
opts.hint: Cost and disruption now; doors open later.

out.text: Certified. Procurement teams stop asking awkward questions.
Some big deals stall at security review.

lesson: Compliance is a cost of selling to large customers. Done once, it becomes a moat against smaller rivals who have not.

title: Free cloud, with strings
text: A cloud provider offers two years of hosting credits if you commit to running only on their platform.

opts.label: Take the credits
opts.hint: Cheaper hosting now; harder to leave later.

out.text: Your hosting bill drops sharply, for now.

opts.label: Stay portable
opts.hint: Pay full price, keep your options.

lesson: Teaser pricing buys lock-in. The real price is what you will pay at renewal, when switching is expensive.

title: A huge order, at a thin price
text: An automaker wants a two-year supply contract worth a third of your output — at 12% below your usual price.

opts.label: Take it
opts.hint: Full plant, thin margin, one dominant customer.

out.text: They go to a lower-cost supplier.

opts.label: Decline
opts.hint: You will not sell at that price.

lesson: Marginal-cost pricing fills idle capacity profitably, but a customer that big will keep asking for the same discount.

title: Customers want local supply
text: After a year of disrupted shipping, several large buyers in {region} want suppliers with plants on their own continent.

opts.label: Pitch them hard
opts.hint: Sales effort aimed at the reshoring wave.

out.text: A couple of enquiries arrive on their own.

lesson: Supply-chain shocks redraw trade maps. Being on the right side of a structural shift is worth more than any efficiency gain.

title: An e-commerce giant calls
text: A large online retailer wants dedicated vehicles and depots for its deliveries in {region}. It would double your volume — and become half your business.

opts.label: Sign
opts.hint: Growth, scale, and one customer with a lot of power.

opts.label: Take part of it
opts.hint: A quarter of their volume, no more.

out.text: A smaller contract and a balanced book.

opts.label: Decline
opts.hint: They will build their own one day anyway.

lesson: Your customer may become your competitor. Customers who can bring a service in-house will, once you have shown them how.

title: Driverless trucks
text: A start-up wants to pilot autonomous trucks on your highway routes. They pay for the trucks; you supply the routes and the data.

opts.label: Run the pilot
opts.hint: Learn early; your drivers will be nervous.

out.text: It works on motorways. You learn a lot.
A near-miss ends the pilot and makes the news.

lesson: Automation pilots are options on the future. Their cost is uncertainty for the people they might replace — manage that or pay for it.

title: This year’s power-contract auction
text: Data centres and utilities are auctioning long-term contracts to buy power at a fixed price, slightly below today’s market. You can bid a slice of your output.

opts.label: Bid a slice of your output
opts.hint: Certain revenue on part of your output, at a lower price.

opts.label: Stay merchant
opts.hint: Sell at market prices and take the swings.

out.text: Your revenue stays tied to the market.

lesson: A long contract turns a risky asset into something like a bond. Each slice you sell gives up some upside for certainty — and certainty is what lowers your cost of capital. Developers sell some output forward and keep some merchant.

title: A transformation mandate
text: A large company wants a two-year transformation programme. It would occupy a quarter of your consultants.

out.text: It goes well and the client renews.
The programme struggles; the client blames you publicly.

opts.label: Bid for the strategy phase only

lesson: Large programmes give revenue stability and concentration risk at the same time. Scope is a risk decision.

title: Big pharma calls
text: A global drug company wants to co-develop your lead programme: cash up front, milestones, and royalties — and control of the late-stage trials.

opts.label: Take the deal
opts.hint: Money now, less upside, less risk.

opts.label: Negotiate for more
opts.hint: They need pipeline as much as you need money.

out.text: You keep control and the funding problem.

lesson: Partnering trades upside for survival. For a cash-hungry developer, a good partner can be worth more than a bigger share of a smaller chance.

title: Added to the index
text: Your shares will be added to a major stock index. Index funds must buy them.

out.text: The share price rises on the flows.

opts.label: Sell new shares into the demand

out.text: Fresh capital at a good price.

lesson: Index inclusion changes who owns you, not what you are worth — but demand for shares is real money in the short run.

title: A university partnership
text: A leading university proposes a joint research centre: their scientists, your problems, shared intellectual property.

opts.label: Fund the centre
opts.hint: Long-term research and a recruiting pipeline.

out.text: Three students work on your problems.

lesson: Basic research rarely pays its own way inside one company. Partnerships share the cost and the knowledge.

title: Talent from anywhere
text: A recruiter offers a team of experienced engineers in a lower-cost city, fully remote.

opts.label: Pass
opts.hint: You prefer people in the room.

lesson: Remote hiring widens the talent pool and narrows the shared context. Both effects are real.

title: A clever financial product
text: Your bank is pitching an interest-rate swap structure that "pays you" while rates stay low. The slides are glossy.

opts.label: Sign up
opts.hint: Free money while rates stay where they are.

out.text: Rates stay low; it pays a little.
Rates rise. The structure costs you a fortune.

opts.label: Ask what happens if rates rise

out.text: The banker changes the subject. You pass.

lesson: If you cannot explain how a financial product makes money for the bank, it is making it from you.

title: A local cause asks for help
text: A children’s hospital in {city} is raising money for a new wing and has asked for your support.

out.text: Your name is on the wing.

lesson: Corporate giving is part reputation, part culture. It works best when it is about the cause rather than the logo.

title: An offer to take you private
text: A buyout fund offers to buy every share at a 30% premium to today’s price. The board must put it to shareholders.

opts.label: Recommend the offer
opts.hint: Sell the company. The game ends here, graded on the price.

out.text: Shareholders accept. The company is sold.

opts.label: Reject it
opts.hint: Back yourself to build more than the fund will pay.

out.text: The fund walks away. Some shareholders are unhappy.

lesson: Selling is a legitimate way to finish. A premium today is certain; the value you might build is not. The right answer depends on what you can do that the buyer cannot.

title: A big tender
text: A large client in {city} has put a two-year programme out to tender. From the shortlist, your chances look like about one in three.

opts.label: Bid a fixed fee
opts.hint: A keen price wins more often, but you carry the risk if the work grows.

out.text: You win, and the project runs to plan.
You win, but the scope grows and the overrun is yours to eat.

opts.label: Bid time and materials
opts.hint: The client pays for the hours: lower odds, no overrun risk.

out.text: You win. The client pays for every hour.

lesson: A consultancy lives on utilisation: people on the bench cost the same as people on projects. Fixed fees win work and shift risk to you; time and materials keep the risk with the client and win less often.
